summary:
AETHRIX — The Atlas of What Remains is an interactive educational app that brings the stories of abandoned NASA hardware to life. Users explore the Moon and Mars, investigate six spacecraft through interactive 3D schematics, and discover how machines left behind helped humanity move forward. Featured artifacts include Surveyor 1, Apollo 11’s Eagle descent stage, Apollo 15’s lunar rover, Viking 1, Sojourner, and Curiosity’s Sky Crane descent stage.

Using NASA planetary maps, mission imagery, and scientific references, AETHRIX connects engineering decisions with discoveries and lasting scientific contributions. Players inspect systems, answer mission questions, and collect lessons in a personal field journal. A simplified Moon and Mars outpost game extends those lessons into decisions about power, life support, food, and crew protection.

Built for the “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” challenge, AETHRIX makes space history accessible through exploration and play. Its offline capability supports reliable classroom and public demonstrations, helping audiences understand why these silent machines still matter.
details:
AETHRIX — The Atlas of What Remains is an interactive educational app that explores the scientific and human significance of NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. It addresses the “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” challenge by turning these machines into stories users can investigate, understand, and connect to future exploration.

The experience begins with a cinematic journey into a freely rotatable planetary atlas. Users explore NASA-textured Moon and Mars globes and locate six featured artifacts: Surveyor 1, Apollo 11’s Eagle descent stage, Apollo 15’s Lunar Roving Vehicle, Viking 1, Sojourner, and Curiosity’s Sky Crane descent stage. Each investigation includes an interactive 3D schematic, three inspectable systems, and a controllable mission sequence. Users connect what they discover to a mission question, receive feedback, and record completed investigations in a field journal.

Scientific information remains inside AETHRIX. Its 37 presentation chapters explain mission purpose, engineering, discoveries, and legacy. A research reader preserves all six supplied research documents and their 37 pages, with original page images, readable text, and notes identifying ambiguous draft claims. NASA resources are incorporated directly: the lunar globe uses imagery and elevation resources from the CGI Moon Kit, the Mars globe uses the Viking global mosaic, and mission presentations include credited NASA photographs, reference images, and artist concepts. Interpretive spacecraft schematics are clearly distinguished from historical evidence.

The Outpost Lab extends exploration into decision-making. Players manage eight planning shifts on the Moon or Mars, distributing power among life support, food production, shelter operations, and science. Forecasts show the consequences before each decision. Darkness, dust, equipment problems, and solar alerts encourage players to balance scientific ambition with essential reserves. These scenarios use clearly disclosed, simplified teaching rules rather than NASA engineering specifications or live forecasts.

AETHRIX was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, and GSAP. Browser storage preserves discoveries and outpost progress without requiring an account. Node.js supports the local presentation version, while the published app runs as a static website. The original ambient score was composed and synthesized with AI assistance using Python and NumPy, then encoded with FFmpeg. Music remains quiet and can be muted.

Development prioritized Intel UHD Graphics 620 hardware, restrained rendering, reduced-motion controls, mobile layouts, keyboard interaction, and an image fallback when 3D is unavailable. A downloadable version bundles the resources for offline presentation. Browser testing covered all six investigations, both outpost scenarios, saved progress, research access, and audio controls.

The intended impact is to make space history approachable through exploration and play. AETHRIX connects the machines’ engineering to the discoveries they enabled, helping audiences see abandoned hardware as a lasting record of ingenuity. AI assistance in code, writing, schematic scenes, and music is disclosed alongside NASA and third-party resource credits.
